reception.text: Individually the proclamations drew little national notice; their phrase "reserved from entry or settlement" appears on four newspaper pages in all of 1902.
Western stockmen, loggers, and homesteaders who lost open range or free timber grumbled, and some western papers and members of Congress were uneasy about reserves made by presidential signature.

political_impact.text: The reserves were run by the General Land Office's Division "R"; Pinchot's Bureau of Forestry could advise only when Interior asked.
The Transfer Act moved the reserves from Interior to Agriculture.
An appropriation act gave the Agriculture bureau the name Forest Service, effective July 1, 1905.
Congress renamed the forest reserves national forests and, in the Fulton Amendment, barred new reserves or additions in six western states except by Act of Congress.

legacy.text: By the Forest Service's reports, the reserves grew from about 47 million acres in 1901 to more than 194 million acres gross by June 30, 1909.
legacy.source: Report of the Forester for 1901; Report of the Forester for 1909
